“können” (can) has “ö”, while “kennen” (to know someone) has “e”. You can hear the difference: “KÖ-nen” with rounded lips.
“w” = “v”: “will” = “vil”. Don't confuse it with English “will” (future)! In German “ich will” = I want.
In words of Greek origin, “Ch” at the start is read “k”: Chor = “kor”, Chaos = “KAH-os”.
Modal verbs have NO ending with ich and er: “ich kann”, “er kann”, “er will” (not “er kannt”, not “er willt”). And the vowel changes in the singular.
“Können” means “can, to be able to” (I have time, I'm allowed, it's possible) and “to know how to” (a skill): “Ich kann schwimmen” = I can swim.
“Wollen” is a firm, direct “to want”. For polite requests use “möchten” (chap. 5): “Ich möchte einen Kaffee”, not “Ich will einen Kaffee” (it sounds like a spoilt child).
As with separable verbs (chap. 6): the conjugated modal goes in position 2, and the second verb, in the infinitive, goes to the END of the sentence:
A separable verb stays in one piece at the end, in the infinitive: “Ich stehe um sechs auf” → “Ich muss um sechs aufstehen”.
Typical mistake: “Ich kann kommen nicht.” Correct: “Ich kann nicht kommen.” The negation “nicht” comes before the infinitive.
To say what you like doing, put “gern” after the verb:
Most of all I like singing.

Mr Brandt knows a lot. He can drive a tram, he can cook, he can play chess and he can name every bus in Berlin. But there's one thing he can't do: he can't use a smartphone.
At Christmas his son, Thomas, gave him a phone. Since then it has been lying in the drawer, next to the old tram tickets.
One Sunday, at breakfast, he takes the phone out of the drawer and puts it on the table, as if it were something dangerous.
Ms Ionescu, can you help me? Thomas wants me to video-call him. He says then I can see my grandchildren. But I don't understand this thing.
Of course I can help you! It's very easy. Look: here you can switch the phone on.
The first lesson lasts an hour. Mr Brandt wants to know everything exactly. What's an app? Why is the phone a camera? And who is this WLAN?
Fritz is lying under the table, asleep. He doesn't want a phone. He wants sausages.
On Wednesday comes the second lesson. Mr Brandt can now write a message. Very slowly, with one finger, but he can. His first message to Lena: “HELLO LENA GRANDPA HERE ROLLS TOMORROW PLEASE TWO”.
Lena replies with three little hearts and a laughing face. Mr Brandt asks: “What do these pictures mean? Is she ill?”
Friday is the big day: the first video call. Mr Brandt sits on the sofa as straight as a candle, wearing his best shirt. Mara presses the green button.
It rings. Then a face appears: Thomas, and behind him three children shouting: “Grandpa! Grandpa! We can see you!”
At first Mr Brandt says nothing. Then he laughs loudly. He holds the phone too close to his face, you can only see his nose, but it doesn't matter.
Mara quietly goes out to the kitchen and makes coffee. From the living room she hears: “And this is Fritz! Fritz, say hello!” Fritz barks once, very politely.

After the call, Mr Brandt says: “Ms Ionescu, I have an idea. You want to speak better German, and I want to understand this phone. You give me phone lessons, and I give you German lessons. With Berlin words! Deal?”
Mara laughs: “Deal! But then let's use “du”, OK? I'm Mara.” Mr Brandt holds out his hand: “Ludwig. But for Fritz I'm still the boss.”
